claims.text: Current experimental and computational methods have limited accuracy, availability, and efficiency for determining high-temperature solid and liquid thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys across large composition spaces.
High-entropy alloys involve a large compositional space.
A single intervention consisting of machine-learning models trained on high-entropy-alloy thermodynamic-property data could overcome these limitations.
The proposed models would be trained on melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change upon melting, and liquid thermodynamic properties.
The intervention applies to high-entropy alloys containing 3-10 principal elements.
Machine-learning models learn patterns and relationships in thermodynamic-property data.
Learning those patterns enables accurate prediction of high-entropy-alloy thermodynamic properties across a large composition space.
The intervention will improve the accuracy of determining melting temperature, fusion properties, melting volume change, and liquid thermodynamic properties.
The intervention will improve the availability of those thermodynamic-property estimates.
The intervention will improve the efficiency of determining those properties.
The machine-learning intervention will reduce prediction error by 20-30% relative to current experimental and computational baselines.
Differential scanning calorimetry and density functional theory are representative current baselines.
Model accuracy may be limited by overfitting, underfitting, and insufficient high-quality training data.
The model can be tested against independent experimental reference data, including differential scanning calorimetry and X-ray diffraction data.
The hypothesis is falsified if model predictions deviate from independent reference data by more than 10%.
